source: Marqu - The Hebrew Gospel of Mark v1.2

verses.translation: Again another time{H6471}, Yeshua{H3442} entered{H935} the house of assembly, and there was{H1961} there one{H259} man{H120} with a withered{H3001} hand{H3027}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יבשה (yeveishah — 'withered/dried', H3001) — the same verb used for the drying of waters (Gen 8:7,14), of vegetation withering (Isa 40:7-8; Joel 1:12), and of Jeroboam's hand withering (1 Kgs 13:4). Greek ἐξηραμμένην ('shriveled') is medical. The Hebrew connects to the Jeroboam episode, where a king's hand withered as divine judgment.
textual_notes: 1 Kings 13:4 — Jeroboam's hand 'withered' (וַתִּיבַשׁ) when he stretched it out against the prophet. Same verb, same body part.

verses.translation: And the Perushim{H6567} were lying in ambush{H693} for him, whether he would heal him on the Shabbat{H7676}, so that they might inform against him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מארבים (me'arvim — 'lying in ambush', H693, from ארב) — a military/predatory verb used for enemies setting an ambush (Josh 8:2,4,12; Judg 9:25,32; 1 Sam 22:8,13). Greek παρετήρουν ('they were watching closely') is passive observation. The Hebrew frames the Perushim as military ambushers; the Greek as careful watchers. A back-translator from Greek would use שומרים ('watching') or צופים ('observing'), not the violent ארב.

Uses שילשינוהו ('they might inform against him', from לשון — 'tongue') — meaning to use the tongue against someone, to denounce or slander. Greek κατηγορήσωσιν ('they might accuse') is a legal term. The Hebrew is more visceral — using the tongue as a weapon.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'lying in ambush' (military). Greek: 'watching closely' (observation). Different characterization of hostility.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559} to the man{H120} with the withered{H3001} hand{H3027}: Rise{H6965} up and stand{H5975} in the midst{H8432}.

And Yeshua{H3442} said{H559} to them: Should a man{H120} do{H6213} good{H2896} on the feast day{H2282} or evil{H7451} — save{H3467} or abandon{H5800} to perish{H6} one{H259} man{H120}? And they were silent{H2790}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses ביום החג ('on the feast day', H2282 from חג — 'pilgrimage feast/festival') where the context and Greek both have 'on the Sabbath' (ἐν τοῖς σάββασιν). The Hebrew uses חג (chag — the word for the three pilgrimage festivals: Pesach, Shavuot, Sukkot) rather than שבת (Shabbat). A back-translator from Greek would use בשבת, not ביום החג. This may reflect a different tradition about when this event occurred.

Uses הושיע (hoshi'a — 'save', H3467, from ישע) — the root of Yeshua's own name. The wordplay is only visible in Hebrew: 'Yeshua' (ישוע — 'salvation') asks about 'saving' (הושיע). Greek σῶσαι ('to save') cannot produce this name-pun.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'on the feast day' (יום החג). Greek: 'on the Sabbath' (σάββασιν). Different sacred day.
translation_notes: 'Save' for hoshi'a — the verbal root of Yeshua's name, creating an implicit wordplay.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} was angered{H7107} because of their deeds{H4639}, as they watched{H5027}, and said{H559} to the man{H120}: Send out{H7971} the hand{H3027}! And it was healed{H7495}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נקצף (niqtsaf — 'was angered', H7107, from קצף) — the verb for divine wrath (Deut 1:34; 9:19; 2 Kgs 5:11; Isa 54:9; 57:16; 64:4). Greek περιβλεψάμενος αὐτοὺς μετ' ὀργῆς ('looking around at them with anger') is a description. The Hebrew uses the specific OT verb for God's fury — placing Yeshua's anger in the category of divine wrath. A back-translator from Greek would use כעס ('angry') or חרה ('burned'), not the divine-wrath verb קצף.
greek_deviations: Greek adds: συλλυπούμενος ἐπὶ τῇ πωρώσει τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν ('grieving at the hardness of their hearts'). Absent from Hebrew.

verses.translation: And immediately the Perushim{H6567} went out{H3318} and took{H6213} counsel{H6098} with those of Herodus against Yeshua{H3442}, that they might kill{H4191} him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שימיתוהו ('that they might kill him', H4191, from מות — 'to die/kill') — the legal execution verb. Greek ἀπολέσωσιν ('destroy/ruin') is broader. The Hebrew specifies judicial killing — putting to death.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} went{H1980} to the sea{H3220} with the students{H8527}, and a great{H7227} multitude was drawn{H4900} with him from Galil{H1551}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נמשכים (nimshachim — 'drawn/attracted', H4900, from משך) — the same magnetic-attraction verb from 2:14. The crowds are 'drawn' to Yeshua as by a force. Greek ἠκολούθησεν ('followed') is simply 'followed.' The Hebrew consistently uses this drawing/attraction metaphor.

verses.translation: From Yerushalayim{H3389} and from Yehudah{H3063} and from Edom{H123} and from across{H5676} the river{H5104} Yarden{H3383} and from Surya and from Sidon{H6721}, for they heard{H8085} of the wonders{H6381} which he does{H6213}, and they came{H935} to him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אדום (Edom, H123) — the biblical name for the region. Greek Ἰδουμαίας ('Idumea') is the Greco-Roman name. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as אדומיה, not use the biblical אדום. The Hebrew preserves the patriarchal name from Genesis (Gen 25:30, 36:1).

Uses הפלאים (ha-pela'im — 'the wonders', H6381, from פלא) — the OT word for God's miraculous acts in the Exodus (Ex 3:20, 15:11; Ps 77:12,15; 78:12). Greek does not have a specific word here — merely ὅσα ἐποίει ('how much he was doing'). The Hebrew identifies Yeshua's acts as divine Exodus-type wonders.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Edom' (biblical name). Greek: 'Idumea' (Greco-Roman name).
Hebrew: 'Surya' (Syria). Greek: Τύρου (Tyre). Different location.

verses.translation: And they went up{H5927} into a small{H6996} boat as the people{H5971} walked{H1980} after him.

greek_deviations: Greek: Yeshua tells his students to have a boat ready so the crowd wouldn't crush him. Hebrew simply says they boarded a small boat.

verses.translation: The sick{H2470} people{H5971} whom he heals{H7495} desired to touch{H5060} him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לנגעו (linga'o — 'to touch him', H5060, from נגע) — the same root that yields נגע (nega — 'plague/affliction', used in Lev 13-14 for skin diseases). The people want to 'touch' (נגע) the healer using the very root that means 'plague.' This wordplay is only visible in Hebrew — the afflicted seek the touch of the one who removes affliction. Greek ἅπτεσθαι ('to touch') carries no such resonance.

verses.translation: And the satan-possessed, when they saw{H7200} him, fell to their knees{H3766} crying out{H6817} and saying{H559}: You are the son{H1121} of God{H433}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כרעו (kar'u — 'fell to their knees/bowed down', H3766) — the verb for kneeling before God (2 Chr 29:29, Ps 95:6) and for enemies falling in defeat (Judg 5:27, Ps 20:9). Greek ἔπιπτον ('fell down') is generic falling. The Hebrew verb implies defeat — the demons kneel in submission.
Uses בן האלוה ('son of God', H433 — eloah, singular) — again the rare singular form. Greek: υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ('Son of God'). Consistent with 1:1 and 2:28.
greek_deviations: Greek has τὰ πνεύματα τὰ ἀκάθαρτα ('the unclean spirits'). Hebrew has המשוטנים ('the satan-possessed'). Different terminology, consistent with ch.1.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} rebuked{H1605} them that they should not reveal{H1540} him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יגלוהו ('reveal him', H1540, from גלה — 'to uncover/reveal/exile'). Greek ἵνα μὴ αὐτὸν φανερὸν ποιήσωσιν ('that they should not make him known'). The Hebrew verb גלה carries the OT sense of prophetic revelation (Amos 3:7 — 'He reveals his secret to his servants the prophets'). The demons' knowledge is treated as unauthorized prophetic revelation.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} went up{H5927} the mountain{H2022} and chose{H977} from those who were most upright{H3474} in his eyes{H5869}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ישרו בעיניו ('were upright in his eyes', H3474+H5869) — the moral criterion of yashar ('straight/upright'), the same word used in Judges for doing what is 'right in one's eyes' (Judg 17:6, 21:25) and for the 'book of Yashar' (Josh 10:13, 2 Sam 1:18). Greek has οὓς ἤθελεν αὐτός ('whom he himself wanted'). The Hebrew gives a moral quality — uprightness — as the selection criterion; the Greek gives only desire. A back-translator from Greek would use רצה ('desired'), not the moral-judgment phrase ישרו בעיניו.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'those most upright in his eyes' (moral criterion). Greek: 'whom he himself wanted' (volitional criterion).

verses.translation: Until there were twelve{H8147}{H6240}, so that they might go{H1980} proclaim{H1875} in the world{H5769}.

greek_deviations: Greek: 'that they might be with him and that he might send them to preach' (ἵνα ὦσιν μετ' αὐτοῦ καὶ ἵνα ἀποστέλλῃ αὐτοὺς κηρύσσειν). Hebrew omits 'being with him' — only the sending to proclaim.

verses.translation: And he gave{H5414} them power to heal{H7495} the sick{H2483} and the satan-possessed.

greek_deviations: Greek: 'authority to cast out demons' (ἐξουσίαν ἐκβάλλειν τὰ δαιμόνια). Hebrew: 'power to heal the sick and the satan-possessed.' Hebrew frames it as healing; Greek as exorcism.

verses.translation: And he placed{H7760} a name{H8034} for Shimon{H8095}: Kefa.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כיפא (Kefa — Aramaic 'rock/stone'). Greek Πέτρον ('Peter' — Greek translation of 'rock'). The Hebrew text preserves the Aramaic name rather than translating it, naturally bilingual. A back-translator from Greek would write פטרוס (Petros) or צור/סלע (tsur/sela — Hebrew 'rock').

verses.translation: And to Elazar{H499} Zavdi{H2067} and to Yochanan{H3110} his brother{H251}, and he called{H7121} a name{H8034} for them — that is [to conclude] — meaning to say: son{H1121} of the Most High{H5945} God{H433}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew names James (Yaakov) as אלעזר (Elazar — 'God has helped', H499). Greek has Ἰάκωβον ('James/Jacob'). The Hebrew uses a completely different name for one of the sons of Zavdi.

CRITICAL: The epithet's meaning is given as בן מהעליון אלוה ('son of the Most High God'). Greek has Βοανηργές, ὅ ἐστιν Υἱοὶ Βροντῆς ('Boanerges — Sons of Thunder'). The Hebrew provides a theological title; the Greek a meteorological one. These are irreconcilable — no back-translator would convert 'Sons of Thunder' into 'Son of the Most High God.' The Hebrew text may preserve a different tradition about the meaning of the name.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'Elazar' for Yaakov. Greek: 'Iacobon' (Jacob/James). Different name.
MAJOR: Hebrew: name means 'Son of the Most High God.' Greek: name means 'Sons of Thunder.' Entirely different etymology.
translation_notes: The bracketed [לסיים] ('to conclude') appears to be a textual gloss or scribal note. The text is partially corrupt.
textual_notes: Uses עליון (Elyon — 'Most High', H5945) — the divine title from Genesis 14:18-22 (Melchizedek's God) and Psalm 82:6, 83:19; Daniel 7:18,22,25,27. This is a theologically loaded OT divine name.

verses.translation: And Andri, and Philip, and Talmai, and Mattityahu{H4993}, and Toma, and Yaakov{H3290} Chalfai, and Tadai, and Shimon{H8095} Qani.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קני (Qani — 'zealous/jealous one') for Shimon's epithet. Greek Καναναῖον ('Cananean'). The Hebrew preserves the meaning — from קנא (qana — 'to be zealous', H7065), connecting to Phinehas's zeal (Num 25:11,13) and Elijah's (1 Kgs 19:10,14).

verses.translation: And Yehudah{H3063} Ashqeriot, who betrayed{H898} him. And after, he came{H935} to the house{H1004}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שבגדו (she-bagdo — 'who betrayed him', H898, from בגד — 'to deal treacherously/betray'). This is the OT covenant-betrayal verb (Judg 9:23, Isa 21:2, 24:16, 33:1; Jer 3:20; Mal 2:10-16). Greek ὃς καὶ παρέδωκεν αὐτόν ('who also handed him over'). The Hebrew uses the covenant-treachery term; the Greek a neutral 'handing over.' A back-translator from Greek would use מסר ('handed over'), not the loaded בגד.

verses.translation: And a great{H7227} people{H5971} assembled{H622} there, so that they were not able to eat{H398} bread{H3899}.
And when those who had not seen{H7200} him went out{H3318}, they said{H559} in their hearts{H3824}: He is honored{H3513}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses נכבד (nichbad — 'honored/important', H3513, from כבד — 'to be heavy/honored'). Greek ἐξέστη ('he has gone out of his mind'). The Hebrew says people honored him; the Greek says his family thought him insane. These are diametrically opposite assessments. No back-translator from Greek 'he's lost his mind' would produce 'he is honored.' This represents a fundamentally different tradition about public reaction.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'He is honored' (נכבד — positive assessment). Greek: 'He has gone out of his mind' (ἐξέστη — negative assessment). Opposite meanings.

verses.translation: And the wise-ones of the law who came{H935} from Yerushalayim{H3389} say{H559} that he is satan-possessed, and by the power{H3581} of Baal Zevuv{H1176} the chief{H8269} of the adversaries{H7854}, he heals{H7495} the satan-possessed.
words: and the wise-ones of the law

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בעל זבוב (Baal Zevuv — 'Lord of Flies', H1176) — the exact OT name from 2 Kings 1:2-3,6,16, the god of Ekron. Greek Βεελζεβούλ ('Beelzebul' — 'Lord of the dwelling/dung') is a modified form. The Hebrew preserves the biblical orthography; the Greek has a variant. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as בעלזבול, not use the OT spelling בעל זבוב.

Uses שר השטנים ('chief of the adversaries', H8269+H7854) — using the Hebrew military title שר ('commander/chief') and the plural 'adversaries' (שטנים). Greek ἄρχοντι τῶν δαιμονίων ('ruler of the demons'). The Hebrew frames the cosmic hierarchy in military terms — a general commanding forces.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Baal Zevuv' (OT spelling). Greek: 'Beelzebul' (modified form).
textual_notes: 2 Kings 1:2 — Ahaziah sent to inquire of 'Baal-Zebub the god of Ekron.' The Hebrew Mark preserves this exact name.

verses.translation: And Yeshua{H3442} called{H7121} them and said{H559} to them in parables{H4912}: How can one adversary{H7854} drive out{H1644} another adversary{H7854}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses משלים (meshalim — 'parables/proverbs', H4912) — the Hebrew genre-word for wisdom comparisons (Prov 1:1, 10:1, 25:1; Ezek 17:2, 24:3). Greek ἐν παραβολαῖς ('in parables') is a direct equivalent, but the Hebrew meshalim carries the full Proverbs/prophetic wisdom tradition.

verses.translation: And if any kingdom{H4467} is without wisdom{H2451}, can that kingdom{H4467} stand{H5975}?

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בזולת החכמה ('without wisdom', H2451). Greek ἐφ' ἑαυτὴν μερισθῇ ('divided against itself'). Entirely different aphorism — the Hebrew says a kingdom without wisdom cannot stand; the Greek says a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand. These are independent proverbs. No back-translator from Greek 'divided against itself' would produce 'without wisdom.' The Hebrew reflects the Proverbs tradition (Prov 11:14, 24:6 — 'without counsel a nation falls').
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'without wisdom.' Greek: 'divided against itself.' Different proverb entirely.
textual_notes: Proverbs 11:14: 'Without counsel (בְּאֵין תַּחְבֻּלוֹת) a people falls.' The Hebrew Gospel echoes this Proverbs pattern.

verses.translation: In a house{H1004} where there is division{H2515} of heart{H3820} among them, it cannot endure{H6965}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חלוקת הלב ('division of the heart', H2515+H3820) — the division is located in the inner being, the heart. Greek ἐφ' ἑαυτὴν μερισθῇ ('divided against itself') is external. The Hebrew internalizes the conflict — the house fails because the hearts within it are divided, not merely because the people are opposed.

verses.translation: And if the Adversary{H7854} rises{H6965} against himself, he is divided{H2505}, and he cannot stand{H5975}, but he shall have an end{H7093}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קץ (qets — 'end', H7093) — the eschatological/apocalyptic term from Daniel (Dan 8:17,19; 11:35,40; 12:4,9,13) for the final end of an age. Greek τέλος ἔχει ('has an end') is neutral. The Hebrew frames the Adversary's end in Danielic apocalyptic terms — this is THE end, not merely 'an end.'

verses.translation: No man{H120} can enter{H935} the house{H1004} of the strong one{H2389} and steal{H1589} the vessels{H3627}, unless he first{H7223} binds{H7194} him, and then he may plunder{H1589} the house{H1004}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כלים (kelim — 'vessels/implements', H3627) — the OT word for Temple vessels (1 Kgs 7:45-51; 2 Kgs 25:14-16; Dan 5:2-3) and household goods (Gen 31:37). Greek σκεύη ('goods/vessels') is equivalent but the Hebrew kelim carries the Temple-vessel resonance — plundering the strong man's house evokes plundering a temple.

Uses קושרו (qoshro — 'binds him', H7194, from קשר — 'to bind/conspire') — the same verb used for conspiracies (1 Kgs 15:27, 16:9, 2 Kgs 15:10). Greek δήσῃ ('bind') is neutral. The Hebrew verb adds the overtone of conspiracy.
textual_notes: Isaiah 49:24-25: 'Can the prey be taken from the mighty (גבור)... Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken.' The strong-man parable echoes this Isaiah passage.

verses.translation: Truths{H571} I say{H559} to you, that all{H3605} the iniquities{H5771} shall be atoned for{H3722}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אמתות (amitot — 'truths', H571, plural of אמת) rather than the Greek amen formula. Greek ἀμήν ('amen') is itself a Hebrew loanword. The Hebrew text uses the full Hebrew word אמת in its plural form rather than the liturgical amen formula — suggesting the author writes from within Hebrew, not borrowing back a loanword.

Uses מכופרים (mechupparim — 'atoned for', H3722) — again the Yom Kippur verb כפר. Greek ἀφεθήσεται ('shall be forgiven'). The Hebrew consistently frames forgiveness as atonement — a priestly act — while the Greek consistently frames it as release.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'truths' (אמתות — plural noun). Greek: 'amen' (ἀμήν — liturgical formula). Different form of the solemn oath.
Hebrew: 'atoned for' (כפר). Greek: 'forgiven' (ἀφίημι). Priestly atonement vs. legal release.

verses.translation: Except for the iniquity{H5771} against the Holy{H6918} Spirit{H7307} — this is one for whom there is no hope{H8615}. This iniquity{H5771} shall not be atoned for{H3722} ever{H5769}, but he is deserving of eternal{H5331} soul{H5315}-death{H4194}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תקוה (tiqvah — 'hope', H8615) — 'there is no hope for him.' This phrase is absent from Greek entirely. The Hebrew adds a declaration of hopelessness with the OT word for hope (Jer 29:11, 31:17; Prov 23:18, 24:14). The concept of losing tiqvah (hope) is deeply OT.

CRITICAL: Uses מיתה נפשיית נצחיית ('eternal soul-death', H4194+H5315+H5331). Greek has ἔνοχός ἐστιν αἰωνίου ἁμαρτήματος ('guilty of eternal sin'). Completely different concept — Hebrew: eternal destruction of the soul; Greek: perpetual state of sin. The Hebrew implies ontological annihilation of the soul; the Greek implies an unresolvable moral condition. A back-translator from Greek would write חטא נצחי ('eternal sin'), not 'soul-death.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'there is no hope for him' — absent from Greek.
MAJOR: Hebrew: 'eternal soul-death' (מיתה נפשיית נצחיית). Greek: 'eternal sin' (αἰωνίου ἁμαρτήματος). Annihilation vs. perpetual guilt.
translation_notes: 'Soul-death' — the Hebrew concept of the soul itself dying, distinct from physical death. This touches on the Hebrew understanding of the soul's mortality or destructibility.

verses.translation: For they said{H559}: He is satan-possessed.

greek_deviations: Greek: 'he has an unclean spirit' (πνεῦμα ἀκάθαρτον ἔχει). Hebrew: 'he is satan-possessed' (משוטן). Consistent terminological difference.

verses.translation: And his mother{H517} and his relatives{H7138} came{H935} and stood{H5975} outside{H2351}, and they desired him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קרוביו (qerovav — 'his relatives', H7138) — a broad kinship term. Greek ἀδελφοὶ αὐτοῦ ('his brothers'). The Hebrew uses the wider 'relatives'; the Greek specifies 'brothers.' A back-translator from Greek would use אחיו ('his brothers'), not קרוביו ('his relatives').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'his relatives' (קרוביו). Greek: 'his brothers' (ἀδελφοί). Broader vs. specific kinship.
Greek adds ἀπέστειλαν πρὸς αὐτὸν καλοῦντες αὐτόν ('they sent to him, calling him'). Hebrew says only 'they desired him.'

verses.translation: And a multitude{H7227} of peoples{H5971} sitting{H3427} around him, and they said{H559} to him: See{H2009}, your mother{H517} and your relatives{H7138} stand{H5975} outside{H2351} and seek{H1245} you.
And he answered{H6030}: Who is my mother{H517} and who are my brothers{H251}?
And he looked{H5027} at those who were around{H5439} him and said{H559}: These are my mother{H517} and my brothers{H251}.
And all{H3605} those who do{H6213} the will{H7522} of the Name{H8034} — they are my brothers{H251} and my sisters.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רצון השם ('the will of the Name', H7522+H8034) — again using השם (HaShem — 'the Name') as the reverential substitute for YHWH. Greek τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ ('the will of God'). Consistent with 1:24 (קדוש השם). A back-translator from Greek would write רצון האלהים ('the will of God'), not the circumlocution השם.
greek_deviations: Hebrew omits 'mother' from the final declaration — only 'brothers and sisters.' Greek includes 'brother and sister and mother' (ἀδελφός μου καὶ ἀδελφὴ καὶ μήτηρ).

chapter_notes.summary: Mark 3 in Hebrew contains major deviations from the Greek text and distinctly Hebraic features. Key markers include: (1) מארבים ('lying in ambush', v.2) using military vocabulary for the Perushim's hostility vs. Greek 'watching'; (2) ביום החג ('on the feast day', v.4) vs. Greek 'on the Sabbath' — different sacred day; (3) נקצף (divine wrath verb, v.5) for Yeshua's anger; (4) בעל זבוב (OT spelling, v.22) vs. Greek 'Beelzebul'; (5) בזולת החכמה ('without wisdom', v.24) vs. Greek 'divided against itself' — different proverb entirely; (6) נכבד ('honored', v.21) vs. Greek 'out of his mind' — opposite assessment; (7) מיתה נפשיית נצחיית ('eternal soul-death', v.29) vs. Greek 'eternal sin'; (8) the epithet meaning 'Son of the Most High God' (v.17) vs. Greek 'Sons of Thunder'; (9) אמתות ('truths', v.28) vs. Greek 'amen'; (10) consistent use of השם (HaShem — 'the Name') for God. The chapter shows a Hebrew text with its own proverb traditions, independent theological vocabulary, and fundamentally different narrative details.
